title: Across the PONs
text:
Public problems rarely respect organizational and capabilities. The collaborative arrangements that form around them, known as purpose-oriented networks (PONs), have become a central instrument of governance, yet we know remarkably little about how their structure and performance vary across national contexts.
Across the PONs is a group of international scholars interested in examining purpose-oriented networks in different national contexts. Where existing research draws overwhelmingly on single-country evidence and single case studies, this project takes a team science approach to build a one of a kind database of PONs. We have developed common survey instruments and interview guides to allow for comparative research across contexts.
Our work combines comparative case analysis with social network analysis to ask what national institutional context does to collaborative governance.
Our hope is that other scholars will join this effort, use our data collection instruments, and contribute to growing database and repository of knowledge on PONs.

title: About the Project
text:
Communities everywhere face problems no single organization can solve such as pandemics, homelessness, flooding, wildfire. Responses to these complex issues tend to be in the form of a coordinated arrangement across levels of government and sectors. Purpose-oriented networks, or PONs, are the formalized version of that response. PONs are defined as three or more organizations that consciously affiliate around a shared purpose.
PONs are everywhere in practice, and they have been studied for decades. But as typically studied, tend to focus on a single network in a single context.
We see the field as having a data problem. Testing whether a proposed relationship holds requires many networks, observed over time, measured the same way. That is data no single scholar and no single lab can assemble. It was this data challenge that gave rise to Across the PONs.

title: About the Project
text:
How the collaborative came together

2022 — Barcelona. A small group of network scholars gathered at ESADE, just emerging from COVID and meeting in person for the first time in over two years. The question on the table was where purpose-oriented network research was headed and what was missing. The proposal made there was a team science one: if enough of us collected data on a few networks each, using a shared instrument, we could build collectively what none of us could build alone. Across the PONs began at that meeting.
2023 — Tilburg. The group assembled a wish list of hypotheses we would test given data on hundreds of networks at multiple points in time, all measured the same way. That list was translated into specific variables and organized into four thematic working groups: context, structure and inputs, governance, and process and outputs. Each group spent the following year determining exactly what to measure and how.
2024 — Chicago. The working groups reconvened to combine their measures and draft the instruments themselves.
Now. Three instruments exist — an interview guide for network managers, a survey for network leaders, and a survey for organizational members — along with their codebooks. They are openly available on the Open Science Framework and have been translated into Spanish and Dutch. The first wave of data collection using these instruments is underway.

The collaborative now includes more than a dozen scholars across the globe, ranging from doctoral students to emeritus professors. A data-use and sharing agreement is being developed to let new members join and contribute to the shared database.

title: About the Project
text:
The current study
The current study applies these instruments to health and human service PONs in four countries: the United States, Mexico, the Netherlands, and Spain. These four were chosen for the variation they offer in two contextual dimensions that theory suggests should matter — how a country provides social welfare, and whether its policymaking runs along corporatist or pluralist lines.
The study asks two questions.
###What country and municipal conditions shape how PONs are configured?
Their size, the diversity of their membership, how they are governed, and what activities they pursue. Most PON research treats networks as closed systems, bracketing the environment they operate in. Drawing on historical institutionalism and population ecology, this aim asks what the environment actually does.

Which configurations are associated with network functioning and performance?
Not which single factor matters most, but which combinations work — since resources, governance, size, composition, and theory of change plausibly operate in concert rather than independently.
That second framing drives our analytic approach. The project uses qualitative comparative analysis, a set-theoretic method that asks which combinations of conditions are associated with an outcome, rather than estimating the average independent effect of each. QCA accommodates an intermediate number of cases, treats each network as a whole configuration rather than a bundle of separable variables, and allows for equifinality — more than one pathway to the same result.

title: About the Project
text:
Why it matters
The result will be a first-of-its-kind comparative database on PONs — qualitative, quantitative, and social network data at organizational, network, municipal, and country levels.
The instruments are open, the protocols are documented, and the sharing agreement will be designed so that other scholars can collect comparable data on PONs in contexts we have not studied. The aim is infrastructure that outlasts any single project, so that the field can effectively test important relationships and guide effective management of these systems.
